tagline: The ocean's top predator, with family dialects and hunting traditions
summary: The largest member of the dolphin family and the most widely distributed whale or dolphin, found in every ocean. Orcas live in tight family groups led by older females, and each population has its own learned calls and hunting methods, from chasing salmon to washing seals off ice floes.
ability: cooperative hunting techniques passed down through families

stats.size: Up to about 9.8 m and 10 tonnes; adult males are larger than females
stats.depth: Often shallow; a tagged whale dived to 1,087 m
stats.range: Every ocean, from polar seas to the tropics; most abundant in cold waters such as the Antarctic, North Atlantic and North Pacific
stats.diet: The most varied of any cetacean, including fish, squid, seals and other whales; each population specialises
stats.conservation: IUCN: Data Deficient (2017); some populations, such as the Southern Residents, are endangered

facts.title: The biggest dolphin
facts.text: Despite its name, the killer whale is the largest member of the dolphin family, Delphinidae. It is found in every ocean, making it the most widely distributed of all whales and dolphins.

facts.title: Diet by tradition
facts.text: Neighbouring populations can eat completely different food. Off the US Pacific Northwest, 'Resident' killer whales eat only fish, mainly salmon, while 'Bigg's' (transient) killer whales hunt mainly marine mammals. NOAA attributes this mostly to culture: learned hunting tactics.

facts.title: Family dialects
facts.text: Among 16 pods of Resident killer whales off British Columbia, each pod used 7–17 types of call. Calls are learned, can stay almost unchanged for more than 25 years, and group the pods into four clans with no calls in common.

facts.title: Making waves
facts.text: Pack-ice killer whales off the Antarctic Peninsula swim side by side towards an ice floe to raise a wave that washes a seal into the water. They took 12 of 14 seal kills this way, choosing Weddell seals almost every time.

facts.title: A dive for stolen fish
facts.text: A satellite-tagged killer whale taking toothfish from fishing lines off South Georgia dived to 1,087 m. After each very deep dive it spent hours making only shallow dives.

facts.title: Long-lived grandmothers
facts.text: Females typically live about 50 years in the wild, but some reach at least 90. Killer whales are among the few animals known to go through menopause.

notes: Slug 'orca'; common name given as 'Orca (Killer Whale)' since NOAA, IUCN and most sources use 'killer whale'. Taxonomy and AphiaID from the WoRMS REST API. IUCN: Data Deficient (Reeves, Pitman & Ford 2017), confirmed via Crossref, GBIF's IUCN category and the IUCN SSC Cetacean Specialist Group status page; several ecotypes may be separate species or subspecies, and the Strait of Gibraltar subpopulation is assessed separately. NOAA gives 32 ft and 11 tons (US), converted to about 9.8 m and 10 tonnes. Depth: the 1,087 m record (Towers et al., published online 2018, in print 2019) was made while the whale was depredating longlines; the paper notes each deep dive was followed by 3.9–4.6 h of shallow (<100 m) diving; no general depth-use figure was sourced. Not shelved as a 'giant'. Pitman & Durban (2012) was published online in 2011. A striking NOAA photo of three killer whales (anim1102) was not used because its Commons record has no description or location.
